label: Behavioral health and human services
description: Organizations that serve people in distress when a community is stressed: crisis line centers and state coordinators, mass care and shelter teams, reunification teams, and child welfare and social service agencies. Variants are the role teams: crisis line, mass care, reunification and child welfare. No state is assumed.

vocabulary.facility: the crisis center, shelter, reunification site or agency office
vocabulary.public: callers and texters, shelter residents, students and families, and children and families served
vocabulary.frontline: crisis counselors, supervisors, shelter staff and volunteers, check-in and release staff, caseworkers
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the crisis center floor, the shelter command post or the county emergency operations center (EOC)

it: crisis contact routing platform (calls, texts and chats from the national network)
shelter registration and daily count reporting
county GIS and EOC incident software
student information system and roster export
statewide child welfare information system and hotline intake
ot: power for electricity-dependent residents (oxygen, mobility, refrigerated medication)
building access control at relocation sites

roles.name: Crisis Center Director
roles.description: Activates the surge plan, arranges overflow and backup, approves public statements and escalates to the state.

roles.name: Shift / Clinical Supervisor
roles.description: Sets queue priorities across calls, texts and chats, rotates breaks, takes consults on high-risk contacts and watches staff wellbeing.

roles.name: Workforce / Operations Manager
roles.description: Owns staffing, call-in lists and schedules, and publishes the queue and wait-time report.

roles.name: Telephony / IT Lead
roles.description: Handles platform outages, routing changes and failover.

roles.name: Crisis Counselor
roles.description: Handles contacts and flags capacity and wellbeing problems to the supervisor.

roles.name: Mobile Crisis Team Lead
roles.description: Sets dispatch priorities for mobile crisis teams and coordinates with 911 and law enforcement.

roles.name: State 988 Coordinator
roles.description: Manages statewide funding, routing and backup arrangements and talks to the national network administrator.

roles.name: Shelter Manager
roles.description: Opens the shelter, sets capacity and rules, staffs it and reports to the EOC.

roles.name: Shelter Health Services Lead
roles.description: Supports medical and functional needs, makes referrals and runs infection control.

roles.name: Shelter Mental Health Lead
roles.description: Provides psychological first aid, supports staff and makes referrals.

roles.name: Disability Integration / FNSS Advisor
roles.description: Advises on accessible space, communication access, durable medical equipment, personal assistance and supervision needs.

roles.name: Registration and Reporting Lead
roles.description: Keeps the resident registry and daily shelter counts and sends data to the shelter database.

roles.name: Mass Care Branch Director (EOC)
roles.description: Chooses sites, opens and closes shelters, places resource requests and plans sheltering for pets.

roles.name: Reunification Site Commander
roles.description: Activates the site, controls flow, holds release authority and handles unaccompanied or unreleased students.

roles.name: Parent Check-in / Release Lead
roles.description: Verifies identity, retrieves students and keeps the release log.

roles.name: Child Welfare Director / Disaster Coordinator
roles.description: Locates displaced children in care, keeps hotline intake running, manages staffing and reports to the state.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Issues public messages and rumor control through the joint information system.

outsideParties: the national 988 network administrator and the federal behavioral health agency
backup crisis centers in other states
the local EOC and emergency manager
the Red Cross and other voluntary organizations
state emergency management and human services agencies
FEMA and the federal behavioral health agency (crisis counseling program)
the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
mediaChannels: the center's official website and status page
school district text and email notices
social media posts that carry wrong numbers or closures

sceneAnchors.public: a gymnasium turned shelter: rows of cots with folded blankets, a registration table by the door with clipboards, hand-lettered signs, volunteers in vests, a pet area behind a rope
sceneAnchors.control: a crisis center floor: rows of headsets and monitors on shared desks, a wall display with blank queues, a whiteboard with a staffing grid, a supervisor standing between rows
sceneAnchors.exterior: a school parking lot with a line of cars and parents standing behind a folding table with signs, volunteers in vests, a bus at the curb, overcast sky

addedThreatFamilies.label: Crisis line surge
addedThreatFamilies.description: A community tragedy, viral media event or anniversary multiplies contacts at a crisis center while staff are short; leadership decides on overflow, rerouting, scripts and staffing.

phaseArc.title: Trigger and first hour
phaseArc.goal: Contacts rise within the hour and the queue starts to build; supervisors see it before the dashboard says so.
beats: A community tragedy dominates local news
Calls and texts double against the same hour last week
Two counselors call out for the evening shift

phaseArc.title: Overflow and backup
phaseArc.goal: Wait times pass the rerouting timers and leadership decides what to switch on.
beats: Unanswered calls begin to reroute to backup centers
Texts and chats queue longer than calls
Spanish-language contacts cannot be rerouted and wait longest

phaseArc.title: Sustained demand and staff wellbeing
phaseArc.goal: Demand stays high for days; staffing, breaks and counselor wellbeing become the constraint.
beats: Counselors on their third long shift ask for relief
A reporter asks for numbers the center has not approved
The state coordinator asks for a briefing

phaseArc.title: Recovery and debrief
phaseArc.goal: Volumes fall; the center restores normal staffing and reviews what held and what did not.
beats: Queue returns to baseline
Overtime and wellbeing check-ins are scheduled
Hot wash covers rerouting timers, scripts and the staffing call-in list

decisionPointExamples: activate the surge plan now, pulling outbound work and callbacks, or hold it and risk a longer queue
request backup support from other centers for texts and chats, or keep contacts local to protect the local answer share
approve a public statement about wait times, or stay quiet while rumors spread
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a rising offered count against the same hour last week, a text queue longer than the call queue, a supervisor note about a counselor who needs a break, a dashboard that lags the floor
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a telephony route that fails over late, a callout the schedule did not plan for, a backup center that is also in surge, a script change that needs sign-off
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state 988 coordinator and the national network administrator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Counts are offered, answered and abandoned by contact type (calls, texts, chats). Routing and rerouting follow the toolkit's dated notes. Contact summaries are fictional and de-identified. Content stays fictional and de-identified; never describe methods or means and never present suicide as a solution; refer only to exercise numbers, never to a real line.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Shelter operations
addedThreatFamilies.description: A general population shelter opens for a hurricane, wildfire, flood or heat and power emergency; residents arrive with oxygen, wheelchairs, medications, pets and service animals and the team must meet needs without a separate tier.

phaseArc.title: Decision to open
phaseArc.goal: The branch director weighs sites, capacity and staffing against the hazard arrival time.
beats: A site list with capacity and backup power status
Staff and supplies are promised but not yet on site
The first evacuees ask where to go

phaseArc.title: Setup and registration
phaseArc.goal: Doors open; registration, space layout and the first needs requests set the pace.
beats: Registration backs up at the door
A resident needs electricity for oxygen
A service animal and an allergy share a room

phaseArc.title: First night and needs
phaseArc.goal: Needs outgrow what was planned: medical, communication access, medications, mental health and supervision.
beats: A resident without a caregiver needs personal assistance
Generator fuel runs lower than planned
An incident report involves a dispute between residents

phaseArc.title: Long stay and closing
phaseArc.goal: Residents stay longer than planned; the team consolidates or closes and plans transition.
beats: A decision to consolidate two shelters
Residents with no home to return to need housing referrals
The closing report is due to the EOC

decisionPointExamples: open the second shelter now or fill the first beyond its stated capacity
assign the limited personal assistance staff to one resident with high need or spread them across several
consolidate two shelters to save staff, moving residents who have just settled
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a registration count that differs from the head count, an oxygen supplier's late delivery, a resident's unrecorded need found on a walk-through, a generator fuel gauge
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a site without accessible restrooms, a supply truck stuck behind a closure, a staff shortage on the overnight shift, a registry system that is down
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the county EOC mass care branch and the voluntary organizations that staff and supply the shelter
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: General population shelters integrate people with access and functional needs; do not invent a separate tier. Residents are fictional, with no real names, addresses or medical record detail. Counts reconcile between the registration list and the daily count.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Family reunification
addedThreatFamilies.description: After a school incident, evacuation or venue emergency, children or patients move from a relocation site back to families while parents arrive faster than staff can verify identity.

phaseArc.title: Incident and site activation
phaseArc.goal: The commander picks a site and roles while parents gather and social media runs ahead of facts.
beats: Students move to a relocation site
Parents arrive at the school before the site is announced
A rumor names the wrong location

phaseArc.title: Check-in and release
phaseArc.goal: Check-in, retrieval and release run; the queue of parents outpaces verification.
beats: Photo identification is missing for some guardians
A guardian is not on the card but is named by the parent
A student has no one coming

phaseArc.title: Exceptions and unreleased students
phaseArc.goal: Cases that do not fit the flow need decisions by the commander.
beats: Two adults claim the same student
A court order is mentioned but not on file
A student asks to stay with a friend's family

phaseArc.title: Close and support
phaseArc.goal: The site closes with every student accounted for; support for students, families and staff continues.
beats: The last student is released
Counselors are offered to families
The district plans a statement and a return to school

decisionPointExamples: release a student to an adult who cannot show identification but is named by a parent on the phone, or hold the student and risk a distressed family
keep parents at the site waiting for verification or send them away and notify by text
close the site with one student unreleased
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a roster that differs from the headcount at the site, a name on the release card that does not match the identification, a social media post naming the wrong site, a late bus manifest
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a text notification system that is slow, a site too small for the line, a roster export that is out of date, a lost release log page
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the school district office, law enforcement and the families' contacts
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Roles are check-in, retrieval, release and exceptions. Release authority is verified by identity, not by assertion. Students and parents are fictional. Do not use trademarked method names as if licensed.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Displaced children in care
addedThreatFamilies.description: A flood, fire or storm displaces foster families and caseworkers; the agency must identify and locate every child, keep the hotline and investigations running and report to the state.

phaseArc.title: Impact and first accounting
phaseArc.goal: The agency starts its plan to identify and locate children in the affected area.
beats: A list of children in care in the affected counties
Caseworkers are displaced too
The hotline gets calls from shelters

phaseArc.title: Locating and contact
phaseArc.goal: Work through the list by method: caseworker contact, provider calls, shelters and schools.
beats: A provider does not answer
A child is found in a shelter with a relative
A placement is lost and needs a new one

phaseArc.title: Continuity and new cases
phaseArc.goal: Keep services and respond to new reports in affected areas.
beats: New reports arrive from a shelter
Court dates and visits are disrupted
Staff stay in contact from temporary locations

phaseArc.title: Reporting and recovery
phaseArc.goal: Report to the state, close gaps and plan recovery.
beats: A child remains unknown after the plan target
The state asks for a status
Recovery plans for placements are drafted

decisionPointExamples: count a child as located on a provider's word or keep trying for direct confirmation
use scarce staff to find the last unknown children or to answer new hotline reports
activate the state disaster plan now or wait for the damage assessment
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a list entry with no recent contact, a shelter registry entry that matches a child, a provider's message that a home is flooded, a caseworker unreachable since the storm
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a records system that is offline, a caseworker evacuated without a laptop, a phone tree with out-of-date numbers, a court hearing that cannot be moved
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state child welfare agency and the shelters' registration teams
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The plan elements are identify, locate and continue services. Children and families are fictional and identified only by exercise codes. No abuse detail is described; refer to a report category only.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Responder and staff stress
addedThreatFamilies.description: A long activation wears down shelter workers, crisis counselors and responders; leaders must notice, support and rotate people while the mission continues.

phaseArc.title: Early signs
phaseArc.goal: Fatigue and irritability appear in the first days.
beats: A supervisor notes a short temper at shift change
A volunteer skips meals
A counselor asks for a different assignment

phaseArc.title: Rising load
phaseArc.goal: Demand and exposure keep rising; breaks slip.
beats: A staff member shows signs of distress
Two shifts overlap with no relief
A manager hesitates to rotate a strong performer

phaseArc.title: Intervention
phaseArc.goal: Leaders apply support actions and rebalance duties.
beats: Psychological first aid is offered by a peer team
A rest area is set up
A rotation schedule is posted

phaseArc.title: Debrief and follow-up
phaseArc.goal: The hot wash covers wellbeing; follow-up is scheduled.
beats: Staff share what helped
Referrals to services are made
Leaders review rotation and relief rules

decisionPointExamples: rotate a high performer out now or keep them on shift through the peak
offer a peer support session during the shift or after it
pull a volunteer who is clearly distressed from a visible role
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a change in a person's behavior at handoff, missed breaks in the log, a peer's quiet comment, a supervisor note about repeated errors
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a shortage of relief staff, a rest area used for storage, a policy that blocks rotation, a manager who does not see the signs
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the organization's own employee support program and the disaster behavioral health team
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use the eight core actions of psychological first aid. Show supportive, practical actions; do not diagnose. Everyone in the scenario is fictional. Content stays fictional and de-identified; never describe methods or means and never present suicide as a solution; refer only to exercise numbers, never to a real line.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Service degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: A telephony or text outage, a staffing shortfall, a cyber incident or misinformation degrades a human services operation that cannot stop.

phaseArc.title: First signs
phaseArc.goal: The operation notices a drop in contacts, a wrong message or a failed route.
beats: A routing failure sends contacts nowhere
A fake closure notice spreads
Staff cannot log in

phaseArc.title: Work-around
phaseArc.goal: Staff improvise while IT and leaders decide what to switch.
beats: Manual logging replaces the system
A backup line is activated
Messages are corrected through official channels

phaseArc.title: Sustained impact
phaseArc.goal: The degradation lasts; services and trust erode.
beats: Backlog builds
A partner asks for status
Staff fatigue grows

phaseArc.title: Restore and review
phaseArc.goal: Services return; the team reconciles records and debriefs.
beats: Records are reconciled
Outage timeline is built
Lessons update the continuity plan

decisionPointExamples: fail over to the backup route now at the cost of some lost contacts, or wait for the vendor's estimate
publish a correction about the false closure from the official account or message partners directly first
move staff from other work to manual logging
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a drop in offered contacts that matches a route change, a partner who reports a wrong number on a flyer, a log-in failure that spreads, a vendor status notice
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a vendor with a long restore estimate, backup phones without the call scripts, a manual log with no template, a misinformation post that outruns the correction
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the platform vendor, the state coordinator and the partners that reference the service
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Keep numbers, route names and times consistent between the vendor notice and the floor. Misinformation uses a fictional or placeholder number, never a real helpline number. Content stays fictional and de-identified; never describe methods or means and never present suicide as a solution; refer only to exercise numbers, never to a real line.

noiseExamples: a donor offering unrelated items the shelter cannot store
a vendor asking about a software renewal
a student asking about a volunteer service-hours form
a reporter asking about last year's budget
a call from a neighbor about a barking dog
pressureExamples: a county official demanding a shelter stay open past its capacity
a parent shouting at the reunification table
a reporter asking for wait times the center has not released
a legislator's aide asking for numbers by the end of the hour
